candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose of soybean presents with symptoms including red to brown dark irregular lesions on stems, pods, and petioles, covered with tiny black spines (setae). The disease is caused by Colletotrichum truncatum and can affect seedlings, leaves, and pods throughout the growing season.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose on soybean includes symptoms such as vein reddening, leaf rolling, shepherd's crook appearance on petioles, brown cankers, and premature defoliation. The fungus Colletotrichum truncatum is the causal agent, with infected areas showing characteristic black setae.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose in Soybean | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose in soybean caused by Colletotrichum species presents with sunken dark brown lesions on cotyledons of seedlings, stem cankers, pod infection that may result in no seed formation, and characteristic setae visible with hand lens. Extension factsheet covers symptoms, pathogen identification, and management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Blight of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial blight of soybean is caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. glycinea. Symptoms include light to dark brown necrotic regions that are vein-limited giving an angular appearance on the young leaves of the plant, often with chlorosis surrounding the necrotic region.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial blight on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Infections begin as small, angular, water-soaked spots that turn yellow and then brown as the tissue dies. The spots darken and are surrounded by yellowish-green halos. Lesions may coalesce to form large, irregularly shaped lesions.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Blight in Soybean | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial blight is caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. glycinea and survives in crop residue. Symptoms include angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn necrotic. Plant resistant varieties and rotate with non-host crops for management.

candidate_sources.title: Extended Version | OSU Soybean Diseases
candidate_sources.snippet: Detailed information on bacterial blight of soybean including symptoms, pathogen biology, disease cycle, and management strategies. Leaf veins may become affected and create necrotic areas resembling lightning on the leaf.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial pustule on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial pustule is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. glycines. Symptoms begin as small, light green spots with raised centers on leaf surfaces. Light-colored pustules often develop in the center of lesions. Disease is favored by warm, wet weather conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Pustule | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial pustule symptoms include small raised spots on leaves and pods. The pathogen Xanthomonas campestris pv. glycines overwinters on crop residue and seeds. Spread occurs through wind-blown rain and mechanical cultivation. Management includes resistant varieties and crop rotation.

candidate_sources.title: Chapter 58: Bacterial Diseases of Soybeans - SDSU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Covers bacterial diseases of soybeans including bacterial pustule caused by Xanthomonas. Symptoms, disease cycle, optimal conditions (86-92°F), and management strategies including resistant cultivars and pathogen-free seed are discussed.

candidate_sources.title: Bean pod mottle virus on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Bean pod mottle virus causes green to yellow mottling of young leaves. In severe infections, leaves may become distorted. Pods can be misshapen with mottling and reduced in size. BPMV is transmitted by leaf-feeding beetles, specifically the bean leaf beetle.

candidate_sources.title: Bean Pod Mottle Virus | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Bean pod mottle is caused by bean pod mottle virus (BPMV). BPMV is a member of the genus Comovirus in the family Comoviridae. The virus is comprised by a bipartite, positive, single-stranded RNA. BPMV can cause yield losses as high as 52% and reduce seed quality.

candidate_sources.title: Bean Pod Mottle Virus | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Bean pod mottle virus causes green to yellow mottling of young leaves. Infected plants may have green stems after the pods have matured. BPMV is transmitted by the bean leaf beetle (Cerotoma trifurcata) with no latent period.

candidate_sources.title: Brown stem rot (BSR) on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Brown stem rot causes browning of the pith in the center of the stem. Phialophora gregata is a soilborne fungus that infects through the roots. Symptoms appear in mid-August. Type A causes pith browning and leaf symptoms; Type B causes only pith browning. Management includes resistant varieties and crop rotation.

candidate_sources.title: Brown Stem Rot of Soybeans (BSR) | NDSU Agriculture
candidate_sources.snippet: NDSU extension guide covering brown stem rot symptoms, pathogen information, disease development, and management strategies for soybeans.

candidate_sources.title: Brown Stem Rot of Soybean | Plant Disease Diagnostics Clinic
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Wisconsin Plant Disease Diagnostics Clinic factsheet on brown stem rot. Covers symptoms including pith browning, leaf discoloration, pathogen Phialophora gregata (Cadophora gregata), and management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Cercospora leaf blight and purple seed stain on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Cercospora leaf blight most often occurs in southern areas of the U.S, but also occurs in the northern Midwest, and can cause severe defoliation of plants and reduce yields, especially in the southern U.S.

candidate_sources.title: Cercospora Leaf Blight of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Cercospora kikuchii is the causal pathogen of Cercospora leaf blight and purple seed stain in soybean. In the presence of light, the pathogen produces a toxin called cercosporin, which is responsible for the purple-bronze discoloration on the leaf surface.

candidate_sources.title: Overview of Cercospora Leaf Blight of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: This publication was developed by the Crop Protection Network, a multi-state and international collaboration of university/provincial extension specialists providing comprehensive information on Cercospora leaf blight.

candidate_sources.title: Charcoal rot on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Charcoal rot is caused by Macrophomina phaseolina, a soilborne fungal pathogen. Hot, dry conditions favor symptom development. Symptoms include wilted plants with gray stems showing tiny black specks resembling charcoal dust.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Charcoal Rot | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet covering charcoal rot in soybean, including symptoms, pathogen information, and management strategies. Caused by Macrophomina phaseolina fungus.

candidate_sources.title: Charcoal Rot in Soybean | Cooperative Extension | University of Delaware
candidate_sources.snippet: Cooperative Extension factsheet on charcoal rot disease in soybean, covering symptoms, pathogen biology, and disease management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Pod and stem blight and phomopsis seed decay on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Pod and stem blight is caused by the fungus Diaporthe phaseolorum var. sojae, while the seed decay is caused primarily by the related fungus Phomopsis longicola or other species.

candidate_sources.title: Stem canker on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Northern stem canker is caused by the fungus Diaporthe phaseolorum var. caulivora, while southern stem canker is caused by the related fungus Diaporthe phaseolorum var. meridionalis. Stem canker can be reduced by planting resistant varieties, delayed planting and foliar fungicides may be beneficial.

candidate_sources.title: A Diagnostic Guide of Diseases Caused by Diaporthe Species in Soybean | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: Diagnostic guide specifically for Diaporthe diseases in soybean published in Plant Health Progress.

candidate_sources.title: Seed Decay and Pod Blight | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: A characteristic sign of pod and stem blight is linear rows of black specks on mature soybean stems. The specks are flask-shaped fruiting structures of the fungus (pycnidia), that may also be present on dry, poorly developed pods.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Diseases: Symptoms, Scouting and Management
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive Iowa State Extension guide covering soybean disease symptoms, scouting and management including Diaporthe diseases

candidate_sources.title: Diaporthe Diseases of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Industry guide covering Diaporthe/Phomopsis disease complex in soybean including symptoms, pathogen information, and management strategies

candidate_sources.title: Frogeye leaf spot on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Frogeye leaf spot is caused by the fungus Cercospora sojina. Symptoms are most visible on leaves with circular to angular lesions (1-5 mm diameter) with gray to light brown centers and dark red-brown margins. The fungus can affect soybeans at any growth stage.

candidate_sources.title: Frogeye Leaf Spot of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Early FLS symptoms are small, dark, water soaked, circular to angular lesions (generally 1-5 mm diameter). As lesions age, the central area becomes gray to light brown with dark, red-brown margins. Caused by Cercospora sojina. Temperature range of 77-86°F (25-30°C) with high humidity (>90% RH) are optimal.

candidate_sources.title: Frogeye Leaf Spot of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Frogeye leaf spot is caused by Cercospora sojina fungus. Symptoms include circular lesions on leaves with characteristic gray centers and reddish-brown borders. Can also occur on stems, pods, and seeds. Provides comprehensive disease management information.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Wilt of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Foliar symptoms include interveinal chlorosis, premature defoliation and wilting. The roots often decay with brown to black epidermal tissues and reddish to brown vascular discoloration extending into the stem.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium root rot on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Root rot appears as reddish-brown to dark brown discolored roots and poor nodulation. If root rot becomes severe, infected soybeans may develop foliar symptoms including stunting, marginal or whole leaf chlorosis (yellowing), wilting, and defoliation.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Root Rot and Wilt of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium wilt is a disease complex caused by several soil-borne fungi, commonly Fusarium oxysporum. More than 10 different Fusarium species are known to cause root rot.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium virguliforme | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on Fusarium virguliforme, the causal agent of sudden death syndrome in soybean.

candidate_sources.title: A Diagnostic Guide for Fusarium Root Rot of Soybean | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: Diagnostic guide for identifying and managing Fusarium root rot of soybean, published in Plant Health Progress by the American Phytopathological Society.

candidate_sources.title: Sudden death syndrome on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet covering sudden death syndrome (SDS) caused by Fusarium virguliforme, including symptoms, pathogen information, and management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Green Stem Syndrome in Soybean | Oklahoma State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Green stem syndrome refers to plants that maintain green stems and sometimes leaves well past the time when they are normally brown and mature. Stems remain green after pods and seeds have ripened. Cause is unknown, potentially linked to stinkbugs, aphids, diseases, or environmental stresses.

candidate_sources.title: Green stem syndrome on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Green stem syndrome occurs when soybean plants maintain green stems and leaves past normal maturity. Plant stems remain moist while pods and seeds have ripened. The cause is unknown but may be related to stress factors, insects, diseases, or environmental conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Symptoms of Stem Diseases Developing in Soybean | University of Maryland Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Overview of various stem diseases in soybean including symptoms and diagnostic information for multiple stem-related disorders.

candidate_sources.title: Diaporthe longicolla (Diaporthe seed decay) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet for Diaporthe longicolla, the causal agent of Phomopsis seed decay and pod and stem blight in soybean. Comprehensive coverage of taxonomy, distribution, symptoms, pathogen characteristics, and management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Diaporthe Seed Decay of Soybean | Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Detailed university guide on Phomopsis/Diaporthe seed decay covering symptoms, disease cycle, pathogen biology, and integrated management strategies for soybean production.

candidate_sources.title: Aggressiveness of Phomopsis longicolla and Other Phomopsis spp. on Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: APS publication examining the aggressiveness of different Phomopsis species on soybean, including pathogenicity studies and species characterization relevant to seed decay and stem blight.

candidate_sources.title: Phyllosticta Leaf Spot of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Phyllosticta leaf spot has low occurrence and minor impact, requiring no management recommendations. The fungus likely survives in infested crop residue and can be seed transmitted, with cool, moist conditions favoring disease development.

candidate_sources.title: Phyllosticta leaf spot | CALS
candidate_sources.snippet: Phyllosticta leaf spot lesions can be circular, oval, and irregular or V-shaped, appearing gray or tan with a narrow, dark margin. Dark specks (pycnidia) develop in the center of lesions. Crop rotation and tillage will reduce survival of the fungus.

candidate_sources.title: Spotting the Right Spot: Frogeye Leaf Spot vs. Phyllosticta Leaf Spot of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Phyllosticta leaf spot is not considered to be an economic threat to soybean. Phyllosticta leaf spot lesions can have dark specks (pycnidia) that develop in the center of lesions, which helps differentiate it from frogeye leaf spot.

candidate_sources.title: Phytophthora root and stem rot on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: This pathogen causes root and stem rot of soybean, with dark brown lesions on lower stems extending from taproot. Disease occurs in poorly drained areas after wet weather. The pathogen is an oomycete (water mold) that produces swimming zoospores in saturated soil conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Phytophthora Damping-off and Root Rot of Soybean | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Detailed factsheet covering Phytophthora damping-off and root rot caused by Phytophthora sojae. Includes pathogen biology, symptoms (dark brown stem lesions, yellowing leaves that stay attached), survival as oospores in soil, and management strategies including resistant varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Phytophthora Root and Stem Rot of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive guide from Crop Protection Network covering Phytophthora root and stem rot of soybean. Details on pathogen Phytophthora sojae (oomycete), characteristic dark brown stem lesions, disease cycle, environmental conditions favoring disease (saturated soil), and integrated management approaches.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Powdery Mildew | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive extension factsheet covering symptoms, pathogen biology, and management of powdery mildew on soybean caused by Erysiphe diffusa

candidate_sources.title: Powdery mildew on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Minnesota Extension resource with details on powdery mildew identification and management for soybean

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Disease Diagnostic Series | NDSU Agriculture
candidate_sources.snippet: North Dakota State University extension publication series covering diagnostic information for soybean diseases including powdery mildew

candidate_sources.title: Cercospora Leaf Blight and Purple Seed Stain of Soybean | NDSU Agriculture
candidate_sources.snippet: Cercospora kikuchii causes both Cercospora leaf blight and purple seed stain. Disease development is favored by high humidity and warm temperatures of 75 to 80°F or higher. The pathogen overwinters on infested debris or seed.

candidate_sources.title: Purple Seed Stain of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Purple Seed Stain caused by Cercospora kikuchii affects soybean seed quality. The disease produces pink to purple discoloration on seed coats ranging from specks to large blotches. The pathogen also causes Cercospora leaf blight with characteristic reddish-purple leaf symptoms.

candidate_sources.title: Pythium Damping-off of Soybean | NDSU Agriculture
candidate_sources.snippet: Pythium damping-off causes stand loss and yield reduction in soybean. The disease is particularly damaging in cool and wet soils. Symptoms include seeds failing to germinate, total disintegration of seed in soil, water-soaked lesions on roots, hypocotyls or cotyledons turning to brown soft rot.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean seed and seedling diseases | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Pythium spp. cause seedling diseases on soybean, leading to preemergence and postemergence damping-off and root rot. The disease is favored by wet and cool soils. Management includes planting good-quality seed in well-drained fields, delaying planting until soils are warmer than 55°F, and using fungicide seed treatments.

candidate_sources.title: Extended Version | OSU Soybean Diseases - Pythium Damping Off and Root Rot
candidate_sources.snippet: At least 27 species of Pythium found in soybean roots, with seven predominant: P. ultimum, P. heterothallicum, P. irregulare, P. attrantheridium, P. sylvaticum, P. perplexum. Infected soybeans exhibit mushy, water-soaked stems at seedling stage. Symptoms include wilting and stunting in patches, particularly in low-lying field areas.

candidate_sources.title: Pythium Seedling Blight and Root Rot of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Pythium spp. is one of major groups of pathogens causing seedling diseases on soybean. P. ultimum var ultimum is particularly important given its aggressiveness, prevalence, and abundance in production fields. Pathogen survives as thick-walled oospores persisting many years in soil. No resistant varieties exist.

candidate_sources.title: Temperature Affects Aggressiveness and Fungicide Sensitivity of Four Pythium spp. that Cause Soybean and Corn Damping Off in Iowa | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Damping off of soybean and corn caused by Pythium spp. is favored by cool temperatures and wet soil conditions. Disease is primarily managed using fungicide seed treatments. Study examines temperature effects on aggressiveness and fungicide sensitivity of Pythium species.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Seedling Diseases | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Multiple seedling diseases affect soybean including Pythium damping-off. Pythiums are fungal-like organisms (Oomycetes) closely related to Phytophthora. The characteristic symptom of Pythium infections is soft, brownish-colored, rotting tissue. Disease management includes cultural practices and seed treatments.

candidate_sources.title: Septoria brown spot | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Septoria brown spot is a common foliar disease of soybean caused by the fungus Septoria glycines. Initial symptoms are small dark brown spots on lower leaves that progress to mid-to-upper canopy. Brown spots enlarge and contain tiny raised pycnidia where spores are produced.

candidate_sources.title: Brown Spot of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Brown spot, caused by Septoria glycines, produces small dark brown spots less than 1/8 inch in size. The first symptoms usually appear on the lower leaves and progress upward. Brown spots often enlarge and grow together into irregular brown areas associated with yellow patches.

candidate_sources.title: Brown Spot of Soybeans | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Brown spot caused by Septoria glycines is one of the most common foliar diseases of soybeans. Symptoms include small dark brown spots on leaves that enlarge and coalesce. The pathogen overwinters in plant debris and spreads via rain splash under warm, humid conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean cyst nematode (SCN) | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Stunting (i.e., reduced plant size) and chlorosis (i.e., leaf yellowing) are the main aboveground symptoms of SCN infection. The female body swells with eggs and initially appears as a small, white pearl or lemon on the root. White (or yellow) females on roots are the only visible sign of SCN infection.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Cyst Nematode: Diagnosis and Management | MU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Soybean cyst nematode diagnosis and management guide covering symptoms, pathogen identification, and control strategies for Missouri soybean growers.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Cyst Nematode of Soybean: A Diagnostic Guide | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: Diagnostic guide for soybean cyst nematode covering pathogen biology, symptoms, and diagnostic procedures published by the American Phytopathological Society.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean dwarf virus | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Soybean dwarf virus (SbDV) was first described in Japan as an agent of severe soybean disease transmitted by the foxglove aphid, Aulacorthum solani, with separable yellowing (Y) and dwarfing (D) strains.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean dwarf virus
candidate_sources.snippet: Soybean dwarf virus causes severe stunting of soybean plants, with leaves that are puckered and show interveinal yellowing. The severity of symptoms depends on the soybean cultivar and virus strain.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Dwarf Virus - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
candidate_sources.snippet: Soybean Dwarf Virus is persistently transmitted by aphids and is endemic in forage legumes in the United States. The virus has two distinct symptom types: Dwarfing strain (SbDV-D) with reduced leaflet size and curling, and Yellowing strain (SbDV-Y) with interveinal yellowing.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Stem Canker | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: NC State Extension publication on soybean stem canker disease with detailed information on symptoms, pathogen identification, and management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Stem Canker of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Crop Protection Network encyclopedia entry on stem canker, a collaborative university resource providing comprehensive information on this soybean disease caused by Diaporthe species, including symptoms and yield impact up to 50% on susceptible cultivars.

candidate_sources.title: Sudden Death Syndrome of Soybean | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Sudden death syndrome (SDS) is caused by the soilborne fungus Fusarium virguliforme. Symptoms include interveinal chlorosis and necrosis on leaves, root rot, and a white pith that distinguishes it from brown stem rot.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Sudden Death Syndrome | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Sudden death syndrome (SDS) is a serious fungal disease of soybean caused by Fusarium virguliforme. Foliar symptoms appear as yellow spots between leaf veins that develop into brown lesions, while roots show necrosis and may have bluish mold.

candidate_sources.title: Tobacco Streak of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Dedicated page on Tobacco Streak Virus in soybean from the Crop Protection Network, covering symptoms, pathogen information, transmission, and disease conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Viruses - Soybean Disease - Soybean Research & Information Network - SRIN
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive resource from the Soybean Research & Information Network discussing viral diseases including Tobacco Streak Virus and other viruses affecting soybean.

candidate_sources.title: Tobacco Streak Virus | Pests & Diseases
candidate_sources.snippet: Dedicated disease library entry for Tobacco Streak Virus with symptoms, pathogen details, and management information from Plantix agricultural platform.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Top Dieback Shows Up in Iowa Again
candidate_sources.snippet: The initial symptoms occur early to mid August as bright yellowing and tissue death on outer leaf margins on leaves in the upper portion of the plant canopy. These symptoms are similar to potassium deficiency, but occur on the upper plant rather than the lower leaves. Discoloration at nodes is followed by leaf edges turning brown, dead tissue falls out leaving a ragged appearance, and eventually the whole leaf dies.

candidate_sources.title: Understanding Soybean Top Dieback
candidate_sources.snippet: Soybean Top Dieback symptoms initially occur in early to mid-August as bright yellowing and tissue death on outer leaf margins on leaves in the upper portion of the plant canopy. The exact cause remains unclear. Although SCN and Phomopsis and Diaporthe spp. have been found in association with these symptoms, there is no proven correlation. Potassium deficiency is commonly associated with low soil test K.

candidate_sources.title: Potassium Deficiency on Upper Soybean Leaves is Not Uncommon during Seed Fill
candidate_sources.snippet: As the deficiency continues and the severity increases, the necrotic leaf margins can simply drop off the plant resulting in a ragged or tattered appearance - Iowa State Extension specialists referred to this condition as 'Soybean Top Dieback'. Affected plants often follow row patterns or field areas, and at maturity, seeds are small and shriveled on severely affected plants.

candidate_sources.title: Sclerotinia Stem Rot (White Mold) of Soybean | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: White mold is caused by the soilborne fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum. Early disease symptoms include water-soaked lesions on the main stem, which can also appear on petioles and pods. White, fluffy mycelium and characteristic black sclerotia are visible on infected areas.

candidate_sources.title: White Mold of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive factsheet covering white mold symptoms, pathogen biology, disease cycle, and management. Symptoms develop from R3 to R6 as gray to white lesions at the nodes, with fluffy white mold during high humidity periods.

candidate_sources.title: Sclerotinia stem rot (white mold) on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Detailed extension guide on white mold caused by Sclerotinia sclerotiorum. Covers symptoms including water-soaked lesions, bleached stems, white mycelium, and black sclerotia formation. Includes management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: White Mold of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: University extension network resource providing comprehensive information on white mold pathogen, symptoms, disease cycle, and management in soybean production systems.
